# SK2184 — The call skips a better overload the derived interface hides

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

An overload declared on a base interface is applicable to these arguments and is a better match than the one the call binds to, and it is unreachable because the derived interface declares the same name.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Correctness |
| Default severity | warning |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | no |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 2.0 |
| ReSharper | `PossibleInterfaceMemberAmbiguity` (`resharper_possible_interface_member_ambiguity_highlighting`) |

## Why

A derived interface that declares any overload of a name takes the whole name: the base interface's overloads of it are removed from the lookup before overload resolution ever runs, so the call binds to the derived one even where the base one is the better match. ⚠ **This was run rather than reasoned about.** With `IChild : IParent`, `IParent.M(string)` and `IChild.M(object)`, `c.M("literal")` executes `IChild.M(object)` while `p.M("literal")` on the same object executes `IParent.M(string)` — the same argument, the same instance, two different methods, and **no diagnostic of any kind** from the compiler or from any `CA*` rule. That is the shape issue #49 describes as "redirect existing calls with no diagnostic anywhere", and it is the only part of the issue that is not already an error.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
interface IParent { void Log(string message); }

interface IChild : IParent { void Log(object value); }

void M(IChild c) => c.Log("started");   // binds to Log(object)
```

Write:

```csharp
interface IParent { void Log(string message); }

interface IChild : IParent { }

void M(IChild c) => c.Log("started");   // binds to Log(string)
```

## When it does not fire

⚠ **The genuinely ambiguous member is a compiler error and is not this rule.** Probed rather than assumed: with `IBoth : ILeft, IRight` where both declare `Value` and `Run()`, `b.Value` is **`CS0229`** and `b.Run()` is **`CS0121`**, both errors — that code does not build, so a rule reporting it would report source no analyzer ever sees. What is left is the case where the binding succeeds and is not the one the reader expects, and only that is reported. ⚠ **Both the applicability test and the betterness test must pass, and together they are what keep `IDictionary` out.** `IDictionary<K,V>.Add(K,V)` hides `ICollection<KeyValuePair<K,V>>.Add(KVP)` — the same mechanism exactly — but the hidden overload takes one argument and the call passes two, so it is not applicable and there is nothing to report. Betterness is decided by conversion and not by heuristic: every parameter of the hidden overload must convert implicitly to the corresponding parameter of the bound one, with at least one of those conversions not an identity. `M(int)` in a derived interface against `M(object)` in the base is therefore silent, because `object` does not convert to `int` and the bound overload was simply the better match. ⚠ **A hidden overload with the *same* signature is not reported**, because that is `CS0108` and the compiler already asks for `new`. Type parameters, `dynamic` and error types are declined; only interface types are inspected, since a class hierarchy makes the same shape visible through its declarations. Report-only: the two repairs are casting the receiver to the base interface at this one site and removing the overload from the derived interface, and which is right depends on what the interface is for. Generated code is excluded.
